The summary is ending: the best sum of a nonempty subarray ending at the immediately previous position. To include the next value, either extend that subarray or abandon it and start fresh. A negative prefix is a burden, while a positive one improves the next choice.
Keep a separate best because the globally best possible subarray may end long before the last element. Initializing with an actual element preserves the nonempty requirement on all-negative input.

Every subarray ending at i either starts at i or extends a subarray ending at i-1. Choosing the better option gives the best possible ending sum by induction. Taking the maximum over all ending positions therefore covers every nonempty subarray. Only two running sums are needed.

concept.question: When is it better to drop the past and start a new continuous section?
intuition: Checking every continuous section recomputes many overlapping sums. A negative accumulated prefix has a simple effect: it makes any section extended from it worse.

At each number, compare extending the previous section with starting fresh at this number. Keep the better total ending here, and separately remember the best total anywhere. This separates the local continuation from the historical answer.
concept.observation: A negative preceding total cannot improve a section beginning at the current number.
approach: Start from the first value so negative-only inputs remain valid.

concept.correctness: Any best section ending at a new number either contains only that number or extends a section ending immediately before it. Extending the best previous ending section is at least as good as extending any weaker one. Comparing these two possibilities therefore gives the exact best ending total. The maximum over all endings is the answer.

complexity.explanation: Read each value once while remembering only the current ending total and the historical largest total. Work is linear, and extra memory is constant.

pitfalls: Return the historical best, not the final ending total.
